catalog_quote: Stress in Unua is not strongly contrastive and it is difficult to distinguish between primary and secondary stress on words of more than two syllables. The observations made about stress placement in this section should be regarded as preliminary. I have not as yet undertaken an analysis of stress placement in sentences and, whilst words elicited in isolation tend to have penultimate stress, it is not clear to me to what extent this stress placement (particularly in words of more than two syllables) is induced as a list reading/reciting pattern. However, some examples of penultimate stress placement in monomorphemic two-syllable words of different syllable shapes are shown in (40): (40) a. 'CVCV: 'baru 'skull' 'baxe 'shark' 'gere 'flying fox' ... b. '(C)VCVC: 'arres 'man' 'batin 'tree' 'bbuxas 'charcoal' ... c. 'CVCCVC: 'bitmos 'bald' 'dabos 'stranger' 'garvat 'fence' ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable (which in disyllables is also the initial syllable), regardless of whether syllables are open or closed; the author explicitly hedges that this is preliminary and based on words elicited in isolation. Google Books snippets of the rest of the section (pp. 37-39, not page-verified) add that some longer nouns have been noted with initial stress, that verbs have main stress on the penult of non-monosyllabic roots, and that the section concludes 'stress is penultimate, except on monosyllabic verb roots which have stress on the root syllable' (p. 39), i.e. the subject prefix on a monosyllabic verb root does not attract stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Author states it is difficult to distinguish primary from secondary stress in words of more than two syllables; no secondary-stress rule given (p. 35).
new_statements.exceptions: From snippets only (pp. 37-39, 391): several multi-syllable words noted with initial stress (e.g., misinov, rroborum; rrirrormien with penultimate); monosyllabic verb roots keep stress on the root syllable rather than the penult (prefix does not attract stress); abe 'where' has initial-syllable stress in isolation but occurs reduced as be (p. 391). Stress described as 'not strongly contrastive'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, words elicited in isolation (citation forms); the author has not analysed stress in sentences and warns that penultimate placement in longer words may be a list-reading artefact. Evidence in (40) is monomorphemic disyllables (CVCV, (C)VCVC, CVCCVC), plus nouns with accreted *na.
new_statements.identity_note: Pearce 2015 describes Unua as spoken on the south-east coast of Malakula (glottocode unua1237, ISO onu); the grammar also notes a closely related variety Pangkumu (referred to in footnotes, e.g. p. 35 fn. 19) but the stress section is about Unua itself. Examples on p. 34-35 distinguish older vs younger speakers for vowels, not for stress.
